Q: lxml python load html string without header and body and add element around targeted elements A:

You can use addprevious before of insert:

imgs = tree.xpath('.//img')
thm = "new-value"
for img in imgs:
    img.set('src', thm)
    a = etree.Element('a', href="#")
    img.addprevious(a)
    a.insert(0, img)

That will result in

>>> etree.tostring(tree)
'<html><body><a href="#"><img src="new-value"/></a></body></html>'

Also, lxml.html.fragment_fromstring can be useful, but you have to provide more diverse example, as in your case of alone image element, it won't be found by your xpath.

See following demo:

>>> import lxml.html
>>> img = lxml.html.fragment_fromstring('<img src="old-value" />')
>>> thm = "new-value"
>>> img.set('src', thm)
>>> a = etree.Element('a', href="#")
>>> a.insert(0, img)
>>> lxml.html.etree.tostring(a)
'<a href="#"><img src="new-value"/></a>'

Update

For a case when img tag has tail, you can reassign it to created a tag:

>>> s = '<html><body><p><img src="old_value"/>some text</p></body></html>'
>>> tree = etree.HTML(s)
>>> imgs = tree.xpath('.//img')
>>> thm = "new-value"
>>> for img in imgs:
...     img.set('src', thm)
...     a = etree.Element('a', href="#")
...     img.addprevious(a)
...     a.insert(0, img)
...     a.tail = img.tail
...     img.tail = ''
...
>>> etree.tostring(tree)
'<html><body><p><a href="#"><img src="new-value"/></a>some text</p></body></html>'

Q: Caddy crashes with an error when configuring Mercure A:

I just needed to create this directory when building caddy.

FROM caddy_prebuild_prod AS caddy_prod
RUN mkdir -p /root/.local/share/caddy/

COPY --from=php_prod /srv/app/public/build /srv/app/public/build

Q: Why mysqldump is returning cannot find table ">" in python subprocess A:

The problem is that python subprocess thinks that the character ">" is the name of your tables so to fix this you have to define the file path name with a flag

I have fixed the problem by using --result-file

subprocess.run(f"mysqldump -u {mysql_user} -p{mysql_password} {database_name} --result-file {file_path_name}.sql")

Q: Extracting data from JSON field containing array data A:

I think you can do this by pre-processing the JSON file to extract array elements before sending to the OTel receiver. This is the most reliable approach since the OpenTelemetry Collector's Transform Processor has limitations when iterating over arrays to create separate log records.

Solution: Pre-process and send to OTel Receiver

  • Use a Python script with the OpenTelemetry SDK to read your JSON file, extract each array element, and forward to the OTel receiver:
import json
from opentelemetry.sdk._logs import LoggerProvider, LoggingHandler
from opentelemetry.sdk._logs.export import BatchLogRecordProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc._log_exporter import OTLPLogExporter
import logging

# Setup OTel Logger Provider
logger_provider = LoggerProvider()
logger_provider.add_log_record_processor(
    BatchLogRecordProcessor(
        OTLPLogExporter(endpoint="localhost:4317", insecure=True)
    )
)

# Create logger
handler = LoggingHandler(logger_provider=logger_provider)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.addHandler(handler)
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

# Read JSON file and extract array elements
with open('logfile.json') as f:
    data = json.load(f)
    
# Send each logRecords array element separately
for record in data['logRecords']:
    logger.info("Log record", extra={'attributes': record})

# Shutdown to flush remaining logs
logger_provider.shutdown()
  • Install dependencies:
pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk opentelemetry-exporter-otlp

Your OTel Collector config would simply receive the logs:

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317

exporters:
  logging:
    loglevel: debug
  # Add your actual exporter here

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [logging]

I think this pattern gives you the most flexibility for processing complex JSON structures with arrays before they reach your OTel collector.

Q: Plotting contours in python in Matplotlib A:

In the case that you have arrays of X, Y and Z values and are just looking to make a contour plot of them, I have found much of the documentation online to be not useful/doesn't explain why Z needs to be formatted the way it is.

Here is some code that works. Z is laid out to better demonstrate a "grid" structure.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x_vals = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
y_vals = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
z_vals = np.array([10, 0, 0, 0, 0,
                   0, 10, 0, 0, 0,
                   0, 0, 10, 0, 0,
                   0, 0, 0, 10, 0,
                   0, 0, 0, 0, 10])

Z = z_vals.reshape(x_vals.shape[0], y_vals.shape[0])

plt.contour(x_vals, y_vals, Z)
plt.show()

And the graph it produces:

One thing that is noted by other responses I've seen is that your Z needs to be the X length * Y length, but the why is often missed, probably because in retrospect this seems obvious - your X and Y values provided to matplotlib will ultimately form a grid, they are not ordered pairs. You need a Z value for each combination of X and Y. In this case, I have 1-5 for my values of X and Y, so I need 25 values to fill in Z in order to make the contour plot. The 2D array structure is so that matplotlib can get those values for each ordered pair in the grid.
